The main aim of this chapter is to familiarize yourself with tidy coding principles. We start by downloading and visualizing stock data before we move to a simple portfolio choice problem. These examples introduce you to our approach of *Tidy Finance*.

## Working with stock market data {#working-with-stock-market-data}

**Exercises:**

1. Download daily prices for one stock market ticker of your choice (e.g. *AAPL*) from Yahoo!Finance. Plot the time series of adjusted closing prices. To download the data you can use the command `download_data` from the `tidyfinance` package (R) or the `tidyfinance` library (Python). If you do not know how to use the functionalities, make sure you read the help file by calling `?download_data`. 
1. Compute daily net returns for the asset and visualize the distribution of daily returns in a histogram using `ggplot2` (R) or `plotnine` (Python). Also, use `geom_vline()` to add a dashed red line that indicates the 5\% quantile of the daily returns within the histogram. 
1. Compute summary statistics (mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum) for the daily returns.

**Solutions:** All tasks are solved and described in detail in the book chapter [Working with stock returns](https://www.tidy-finance.org/chapters/working-with-stock-returns.html).

## Scaling up the analysis {#scaling-up-the-analysis}

As a next step, we generalize the code from before such that all the computations can handle an arbitrary vector of tickers (e.g., all constituents of an index). Following tidy principles, it is quite easy to download the data, plot the price time series, and tabulate the summary statistics for an arbitrary number of assets.

**Exercises:**

1. Now the tidyverse magic starts: Take your code from before and generalize it such all the computations are performed for an arbitrary vector of tickers (e.g., `ticker <- c("AAPL", "MMM", "BA")` (R) or `ticker = ["AAPL", "MMM", "BA"]` (Python)). Automate the download, the plot of the price time series, and create a table of return summary statistics for this arbitrary number of assets.
1. Consider the research question *Are days with high aggregate trading volume often followed by high aggregate trading volume days?* How would you investigate this question? Hint: Compute the aggregate daily trading volume (in USD) and find an appropriate visualization to analyze the question.
1. Ask yourself how the visualization could be improved by adding further information (e.g., highlighting days with extreme trading volume), improving axis labels, changing the style (colors, themes, etc.). Implement your ideas and create a final version of the plot. Make sure the plot is self-explanatory (e.g., contains captions, legends, an appropriate title, etc.).


**Solutions:** All tasks are solved and described in detail in the sections [Scaling up the analysis](https://www.tidy-finance.org/chapters/working-with-stock-returns.html#scaling-up-the-analysis) and [Other forms of data aggregation](https://www.tidy-finance.org/chapters/working-with-stock-returns.html#other-forms-of-data-aggregation) of the book chapter *Working with stock returns*.

## Accessing and managing financial data {#financial-data}

**Exercises:**

1. Read the book chapters [Accessing and managing financial data](https://www.tidy-finance.org/chapters/accessing-and-managing-financial-data.html) and [WRDS, CRSP, and Compustat](https://www.tidy-finance.org/chapters/wrds-crsp-and-compustat.html) entirely; both show the R and the Python code side by side. They describe almost every dataset that matters for research in empirical finance. Since CRSP's update in July 2022, monthly returns already include delisting returns, so you no longer need to adjust for delistings yourself; the second chapter explains the details.

2. The `data` folder of your course repository already contains the public data of the first chapter, so everyone in the course works with the same numbers: the Fama-French three factors (`factors_ff3_monthly.parquet`), the ten industry portfolios (`industries_ff_monthly.parquet`), the macroeconomic predictors of Welch and Goyal (`macro_predictors.parquet`), and the consumer price index (`cpi_monthly.parquet`). Download the CRSP data, `crsp_monthly.parquet`, from Absalon and store it in the same folder under exactly this name. The CRSP data are licensed: Git ignores the file, so it never ends up on GitHub. Later in the course, `stock_characteristics_monthly.parquet` follows the same way.

3. Almost all exercises from now on start by reading data from these files. This is all it takes, from a fresh R or Python session:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R

```{r}
#| label: r-load-crsp-monthly
#| eval: false
library(nanoparquet)

crsp_monthly <- read_parquet("data/crsp_monthly.parquet")
```

## Python

```{python}
#| label: py-load-crsp-monthly
#| eval: false
import polars as pl

crsp_monthly = pl.read_parquet("data/crsp_monthly.parquet")
```

:::

4. Replicate the figure from the lecture slides that shows the number of stocks in the CRSP sample over time, by listing exchange (NYSE, NYSE American, formerly AMEX, and Nasdaq).

**Solutions:** The book chapter [WRDS, CRSP, and Compustat](https://www.tidy-finance.org/chapters/wrds-crsp-and-compustat.html) solves the figure in R and Python; the lecture slides show it as well.
